Introduction to the Theory of Computation

Can a computer think? What can computer solve? What kind of problems can a computer solve efficiently and practically? All these questions are philosophical. But "computer" is a vague wordings - is a vending machine a computer? Or an electronic calculator? Or some sort of teletype printer? Or even abacus? As you can see - we need some sort of clear definition of "computer" and "problem" to reason about them.

Following Aristotle, we use computational models, a model that supports a certain set of primitive operations, as an abstraction of computers.
  • Part One goes through weaker automata, such as the Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA), Non-deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA) and the Pushdown Automaton (PDA).
  • In Part Two and Three, we focus on the strongest known implementable model to human kind - the Turing Machine (TM).
    • Part Two focuses on Computability Theory, which asks the question - What class of problems can be solved by Turing Machine?
    • Part Three focuses on Complexity Theory, which raises a similar question - What class of problems can be solved efficiently, measured in time or space, by Turing Machine?

All these questions can be somewhat answered via precise and elegant set-theoric definitions and deductions.

Part One: Automata and Languages

Formal Languages and Decision Problems

A finite alphabet \( \Sigma \) as any set of symbols such as \( \{ \texttt{0}, \texttt{1} \} \) or \( \{ \texttt{a}, \texttt{b}, \texttt{c} \} \). A string over \( \Sigma \) is any finite sequence of symbols of \( \Sigma \) such as \( \texttt{000101} \) or \( \texttt{ababc} \), where the empty string is denoted as \( \varepsilon \). The set of all strings over \( \Sigma \) is denoted as \( \Sigma^* \). Finally, a language \( L \) over \( \Sigma \) is any collection (set) of strings over \( \Sigma \).

A large class of problems that we will deal with is the decision problems - That is, given a language \( L \) and any string \( w \), decide if \( w \in L \). For example, let \( L = \{ \texttt{a}^n \texttt{b}^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \} \), then \( \texttt{aabb} \in L \) and \( \varepsilon \in L \), but \( \texttt{aab} \not\in L \). We want our machines to be able to decide that for us. When is it possible, and when is it not? That depends on the language given. And, our particular choice of computational model. The more complicated a language is, then more strength our model requires to solve the decision problem.

Naturally, we want classify the languages according to how "complicated" they are, and the computational models according to their ability in recognizing languages. In Part One, we will go through Regular Languages (RL) and Context-Free Languages (CFL) as the simplest classes of languages.

Regular Languages

Informally, every machine requires some "memory" to store the intermediate computational results. First, we assume the memory is finite, that is, the number of states of the machine is finite - Finite Automata. What can such a machine do? Let's say the characters of the input is read one-by-one. Then, the transition to the next state should only depends on the previous state and the current character. Finally, we should accept or reject a string base on the final state only.

The machine described above is called the Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA). To formally capture the intuition, we can define a DFA as a 5-tuple \( M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F) \), where
  1. \( Q \) is a finite set called states,
  2. \( \Sigma \) is a finite set called alphabet,
  3. \( \delta: Q \times \Sigma \to Q \) is the transition function,
  4. \( q_0 \in Q \) is the start state (or initial state), and
  5. \( F \subseteq Q \) is the set of accept states.

One may specify the DFA by drawing out the state diagram (directed graph with arrow represents \( \delta \)), or alternatively use a table to represent transition \( \delta \). The input string \( w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n \) is in \( \Sigma^* \). The start state is \( r_0 = q_0 \), where we let \( r_k = \delta(r_{k - 1}, w_k) \) for \( 1 \le k \le n \). We accept \( w \) if and only if the final state \( r_n \in F \). We say the DFA \( M \) recognizes language \( A \) iff \( A = L(M) = \{ w \in \Sigma^* \, \vert \, M \text{ accepts } w \} \). We say a language is regular iff it can be recognized by some DFA.

Can we make our machine more powerful under the restriction of finite states? Let's say we allow non-determinism and \( \varepsilon \)-transition:
  • Non-determinism: We can choose non-deterministically one of multiple (or none) states to go to, upon receiving a character.
  • \( \varepsilon \)-transitions: We can transit on \( \varepsilon \)-transitions freely, without consuming any character.
We accept a string \( w \) iff there exists a walk that consumes all of \( w \), and ends up at any accept state. This is called Non-deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA), and the only difference from DFA is that we define \( \delta: Q \times \Sigma_{\varepsilon} := \Sigma \cup \{ \varepsilon \} \to \mathcal{P}(Q) \) instead, where \( \mathcal{P}(Q) \) is the power set of \( Q \).

Turns out the computational power of DFA and NFA are equivalent! That is, if a language \( L \) can be recognized by a DFA, then there exists a NFA that can recognize \( L \) as well, and vice versa. Clearly NFA is more powerful than DFA, while the reduction from NFA to DFA can be done by a clever trick - simply treat the NFA with states \( Q \) as a DFA on the states \( \mathcal{P}(Q) \). Although it takes exponentially more resources, we don't care (for now) since we just care whether it is computable using a certain computational model.

Both DFA and NFA can be used to recognize regular languages. There is another way to attack this - can we specify a way to express all the strings in a regular language? For example, we can use \( \texttt{(01)}^* \) to represent \( \{ \texttt{(01)}^{n} \, \vert \, n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \} \). We want to have a set of "regular" operations on languages such that it can generates all regular language, but none the others. How can we achieve that?

Turns out the set of regular operations we need is union (\( A \cup B \)), concatenation (\( A \circ B \)) and star (\( A^* \)). More formally, we define
  1. Union: \( A \cup B = \{ x \sep x \in A \text{ or } x \in B \} \)
  2. Concatenation: \( A \circ B = \{ xy \sep x \in A \text{ and } x \in B \} \)
  3. Star: \( A^* = \{ x_1x_2 \dots x_k \sep k \ge 0 \text{ and each } x_i \in A \} \)
Then regular expression is all the we can made up with character \( a \in \Sigma \) (represents \( \{ a \}\)), empty string \( \varepsilon \) (represents \( \{ \varepsilon \} \)), empty set \( \varnothing \) and these three regular operations. Each such regular expression represents a language. For simplicity, we usually write \( A^+ = AA^* \) and \( A^k \) as \( k \) copies of \( A \) concatenate together.

Turns out NFA and regular expression has the same computational power as well! That is, each regular expression represents a regular language, and we can represent all regular languages this way. How shall we prove this? First, let's consider the easier direction - given a regular expression \( R \), construct a NFA that recgonize \( L(R) \). Note that \( R \) is defined inductively by merging smaller expressions together, we only have to show that for regular expressions \( R_1 \) and \( R_2 \), \( L(R_1) \cup L(R_2) \), \( L(R_1) \circ L(R_2) \) and \( L(R_1)^* \) are all regular languages. Simply consider the NFAs that recognize \( L(R_1) \) and \( L(R_2) \) respectively, then we can use them as components to build NFA that recognize the combined language. This also shows regular languages is closed under union, concatenation and star. For the other direction, we can convert NFA to Generalised Non-deterministic Finite Automaton (GNFA) - a state digram where each edge is a regular expression, with one accept state only. We can then simply remove the nodes one-by-one to obtain the regular expression between the start state and accept state.

Since DFA, NFA and regular expression are equivalent in their computational power, when we work with proofs on regular languages, we may pick the easiest one to work with. For example, one may use DFA to show regular languages are closed under complement and intersection, which is hard (if not impossible) to prove with NFA, while for regular operations it is much easier to work with NFA.

Finally, how can we show some language, say \( L = \{ \texttt{a}^{n} \texttt{b}^n \sep n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \} \), is not regular? We have the pumping lemma for regular languages: Consider a DFA \( M \) which recognizes language \( L = L(M) \). By running it on any sufficiently long string \( w \), \( M \) must eventually reach some state that previously reached. Hence, for any sufficiently large \( p \) with \( |w| \ge p \), there exists a decomposition \( w = xyz \) where \( |xy| \le p \), \( |y| \ge 1 \) and \( xy^nz \in L(M) \) for all \( n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \). We can "pump" the middle part of the string indefinitely, hence the name of pumping lemma. We may use this lemma to induce contradictions from the regularity assumption of languages.
